text: Extraction, inversion, and membership inference all share one hard dependency: volume. None of them work in a handful of requests. That single fact is why this lesson's defenses are so effective — they don't need to detect intent, they just need to raise the cost of doing anything at the scale these attacks require.

Rate limiting is the highest-leverage control here, and it's the most familiar one in API security: per-key or per-account query quotas sized to what a legitimate integration actually needs, progressive throttling that slows response times as a caller approaches their limit instead of a hard cliff, and step-up friction like CAPTCHAs once volume crosses what's normal for a real user. This is the same discipline from Course 10's API security content, pointed at a new asset — the model's decision boundary.

Volume alone isn't the only signal worth watching. Extraction and inversion leave a shape in query logs: near-duplicate queries that vary one feature at a time, systematic grid-like sweeps across the input space, and traffic disproportionately clustered right where confidence sits near fifty-fifty — exactly where a substitute model needs the most training signal. Feeding that into the same SIEM and anomaly-detection pipeline that already watches for credential stuffing closes the gap volume limits alone can miss.

Rate limiting controls how many queries a caller can make. Output minimization controls how much each query is worth to them. Returning only the top label instead of a full confidence vector, or coarsening a score to high, medium, or low, preserves what a legitimate caller actually needs while destroying the fine-grained gradient signal both extraction and inversion depend on.

A small calibrated perturbation on repeated near-identical queries is a lightweight relative of a much stronger guarantee: differential privacy, which bounds mathematically how much any single training record can ever influence a model's output. That's where the next lesson picks up — moving from operational controls to a guarantee you can actually prove.
